title: Palestine Action activists to appeal terror sentencing
summary:
Palestine Action activists to appeal terror sentencing

Submitted by Katherine Hearst on Thu, 09/03/2026 - 15:29
The four activists, the first direct action protesters to be sentenced as terrorists, argue that their sentences are 'manifestly excessive'
Sukaina Rajwani, defendant Fatema Rajwani's mother, stands with Emma Kamio, Leona 'Ellie' Kamio's mother, 3 September 2026 (Katherine Hearst/MEE)
Off

Four Palestine Action activists will appeal their sentencing by a UK court as terrorists for their role in a raid on an Israeli-owned arms factory.

In May, Charlotte ‘Lottie’ Head, Fatema Rajwani, Leona ‘Ellie’ Kamio and Samuel Corner were convicted by jurors of criminal damage charges for smashing up Israeli weapons - including quadcopter drones - in an Elbit Systems factory near Bristol in August 2024.

In an unprecedented ruling in June, the presiding judge, Justice Johnson, determined that their offences carried a "terrorist connection", handing them sentences ranging from four to eight years.

They became the first direct action protesters convicted of criminal charges to be sentenced as terrorists.

Throughout the trial, they were barred from telling jurors of the potential terror designation and from speaking about their motivations for damaging weapons intended for use by Israel in Gaza.

Simon Natas, partner at ITN Solicitors who represents the four prisoners, confirmed at a press conference on Thursday that they will appeal their sentences as "manifestly excessive", arguing that Johnson wrongfully applied the terrorist connection to their case.

Behind bars

Sukaina Rajwani, the mother of the youngest defendant, 22-year-old Fatema Rajwani, told a press conference on Thursday that her daughter had already spent "10 percent of her life behind bars".

Rajwani, Kamio, Head and Corner are now locked up as high-risk prisoners. Head, Kamio and Rajwani have been separated from one another and moved to different prisons.

Zionism has warped the lexicon, so words are now convenient weapons
Read More »

Rajwani said that, as a terrorist prisoner, her daughter will only be permitted contact with 20 individuals who have to be vetted.

"This will cut her off from most of her family, friends and support network," she said.

Rajwani told Middle East Eye that the vetting process for her daughter’s contact list is already under way.

"She had to pick 20 people," she added. "These 20 people have a weight to bear. They have to be available; they have to be committed. They have to be happy to be screened so diligently by the government."

Rajwani said that her daughter had just been moved from HMP Bronzefield, where she was held with Head and Kamio, to HMP Send.

Emma Kamio, defendant Charlotte Kamio's mother, told reporters that her daughter was 28 years old "when she took action as a Forest nursery school teacher", but that "she will be 50 years old before state harassment ends for her".

The terror connection not only lengthens their sentences but will mean they will be subject to stringent restrictions for decades after release.

She said the designation will also bar her daughter from working with children.

A very high bar

The appeal argues that Johnson wrongfully relied on a financial report commissioned by the insurers of Elbit systems as evidence that the defendants had caused "serious harm".

Johnson said in his ruling that the determination was made on the basis that the defendants caused "serious property damage", with the intention of influencing the UK government and "intimidating a section of the public". 

The Terrorism Act 2000 defines terrorism as "the use or threat, for the purpose of advancing a political, religious or ideological cause, of action which involves serious violence against any person or property". 

Natas said the legislation provides little clarity on what constitutes "serious damage", adding that there is also scarce case law as guidance for making the determination.

'[My daughter] will be 50 years old before state harassment ends for her'

- Emma Kamio, Leona ‘Ellie’ Kamio's mother

When introducing the legislation in 1999, then-Home Secretary Jack Straw said that an act of terror would have to involve "the threat of use of serious violence" and be designed to create a "climate of extreme fear".

"That sets the bar for what terrorism is very, very high," Natas said. 

Natas, who has worked on protest cases for over 15 years, said : "It would have been unthinkable to anyone involved in those cases that they would ever have been considered there being a terrorist connection".

The activists were cleared of all violence-related allegations, including aggravated burglary and violent disorder. Johnson’s finding of a terrorist connection relates only to the criminal damage charge they were convicted of. Corner’s grievous bodily harm conviction was not sentenced as having a terror connection.

"We also say there was no intention to influence the government," Natas told reporters. "The intention here was simply to damage weapons to stop them being sent to Israel."

The appeal also argues that the "terrorist connection scheme" is incompatible with Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which stipulates that a "heavier penalty" cannot be imposed than "the one that was applicable at the time the criminal offence was committed".

It also contends that Johnson’s finding contravenes Article 6 of the ECHR, which enshrines the right to a fair and impartial trial.

The defendants’ legal team is awaiting permission to appeal and a hearing date to be confirmed.

title: Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defence ties with Israel
summary:
Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defence ties with Israel

Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defence bill provision that would deepen US-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing US skepticism toward the longtime ally.

The provision would deepen cooperation between the US and Israeli defence sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.

The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and US-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli weapons industry.

In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defence sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.

The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups. 

"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the US defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter.

title: US diplomat Boulos won't name 'at least 12 countries' involved in Sudan war
summary:
US diplomat Boulos won't name 'at least 12 countries' involved in Sudan war

Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Thu, 09/03/2026 - 15:51
Trump adviser does not name UAE, Egypt or Turkey, saying 'we are not here to go into these details'
Massad Boulos, senior advisor to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs, speaks with the media outside the White House in Washington, DC, 21 July 2026 (AFP)
Off

US President Donald Trump’s senior adviser on African and Arab affairs has said “at least 12 countries” are involved in the Sudan war but has declined to name them.

Massad Boulos, whose son Michael is married to Trump’s daughter Tiffany, told the BBC’s Focus on Africa that “all of the neighbouring countries in the region are participating in one way or another, or facilitating certain acts” in the war.

“As for the military support, this is done currently by all the neighbouring countries in addition to some other regional actors. This is really very sad,” Boulos said. 

“We are not going to go into names at this time, but I think they are well known. There are probably at least 12 countries that are in one way or another providing military support,” the Lebanese-born US diplomat said.

When asked by reporter Waihiga Mwaura why the United States was not willing to name the countries supplying the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Boulos said there was “no hesitation” and returned to talking about Washington’s plan to apply an arms embargo to Sudan.

There is currently a UN arms embargo on Darfur, the vast western region of Sudan that serves as the RSF’s powerbase and which was where the paramilitary’s forerunner, the Janjaweed militias, slaughtered hundreds of thousands of civilians in the first decade of this century.

The embargo has been in place for more than 20 years but is set to expire on 12 September. Middle East Eye understands that UN Security Council members received the final report from the UN Panel of Experts on 13 July and that this report contains further evidence that the United Arab Emirates has violated the embargo.

UAE involvement in Sudan

The UAE has consistently denied supporting the RSF throughout the Sudan war, which began in April 2023 and has led to the largest humanitarian crisis in the world. 

But UN experts, human rights groups and Middle East Eye have all reported extensively on Emirati support for the Sudanese paramilitary, which is led by former Janjaweed leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo and has been widely accused of committing genocide in Darfur.

Weapons serial numbers, flight tracking logs, military hardware recovered from the battlefield and a wide array of sources all attest to the UAE’s support for the RSF, which is most usually routed through Libya, Chad, Ethiopia, and Somaliland. 

Exclusive: The Ethiopian army base covertly supporting Sudan’s RSF
Read More »

MEE also understands that the Panel of Experts report adds detail to already widely reported accusations relating to Colombian mercenaries contracted by the UAE to fight for the RSF in Sudan.

Asked about the UAE, Boulos said he met with the Emiratis regularly, including last week. “Their position is that they deny any direct involvement,” he said, of Emirati support for the RSF.

“There might be some traders or whatever that are doing these sorts of supplies, providing supplies to both sides, but again we are not here to go into these details.”

While the UAE backs the RSF, Egypt and Turkey are the primary military backers of the SAF. Turkish sources have confirmed to MEE that their country is supplying the Sudanese army with drones, ammunition and air defence systems. 

Turkish drone operators have been on the ground in Sudan, and Turkey has, alongside Egypt, bombed convoys supplying the RSF in the triangle border region that includes remote desert areas of Sudan, Libya and Egypt. 

Boulos told the BBC that a nationwide arms embargo in Sudan would ban the sale, transfer or supply of weapons and military equipment to all sides of the conflict. 

“We have to act, we have to do something about it and that’s why I talked to the members of the Security Council about it, Boulos said, though he sounded less confident about the UNSC passing a resolution on a nationwide embargo – Russia has used its veto to block similar efforts. 

The US diplomat said that his call for an arms embargo came “in the context of the increasing levels of military support that we have seen to both warring parties in the recent weeks and months. There’s a tremendous increase to both sides.”

title: Death toll from Israeli settler attacks spirals in 'most violent' year for West Bank
summary:
Death toll from Israeli settler attacks spirals in 'most violent' year for West Bank

During a settler attack aimed at stealing sheep, the Israeli army killed a Palestinian boy and a young man on Wednesday evening in the village of Al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Omar Muhammad Na’san, 19, and Khalil Rasem Shahada, 16, were shot dead by Israeli soldiers.

Marzouq Abu Na’im, a member of the village council and an activist documenting settler attacks there, told Middle East Eye that armed settlers attacked a house to steal livestock. The Israeli army then stormed the village to provide protection for the settlers and took up positions on the roof of the targeted house.

In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses."

The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. title: Israel returns body of Palestinian teenager it killed in 2025
summary:
Israel returns body of Palestinian teenager it killed in 2025

Israel has returned the body of 15-year-old Palestinian Jadallah Jihad Jumaa Jadallah, whom its forces shot dead in November 2025.

Palestinian authorities received his remains in the occupied West Bank months after his killing, according to the Wafa news agency.

Jadallah’s family will now make arrangements for his burial. He lived in the Far’a refugee camp.

Israel has long withheld the bodies of Palestinians, inflicting further suffering on families seeking to bury their loved ones. Some Palestinian families have waited decades for Israel to return their relatives’ remains.

title: How Israel armed Argentina to kill British soldiers during Falklands War
summary:

Tensions between Britain and Israel are rapidly escalating with Andy Burnham's government gearing up to announce a raft of strong measures on the occupied West Bank, including a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements.

Israel has released five Lebanese men its forces detained in areas under military control in southern Lebanon, according to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office.

title: Ben Gvir set to unveil $20bn plan to ethnically cleanse Gaza within seven years
summary:
Ben Gvir set to unveil $20bn plan to ethnically cleanse Gaza within seven years

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Thu, 09/03/2026 - 12:35
The far-right leader will make the plan a condition for joining any future Israeli coalition
Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir (C) storms Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem on 23 July 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir will unveil a plan on Thursday to "encourage voluntary emigration from Gaza", making it a central plank of his election campaign and a key demand for joining any future coalition.

Ben Gvir, who leads the Jewish supremacist Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, has called the ethnic cleansing plan “Disengagement 710”.

Israeli media reports that the far-right minister has spent months developing the proposal, which aims to force 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza during its first year.

Within three years, Israel would forcibly transfer 1.11 million Palestinians from their land. By the end of the seven-year programme, that figure would reach about 1.86 million.

Israel has already paved the way for such a plan by destroying or damaging more than 80 percent of Gaza’s homes, businesses, schools, universities and hospitals, while also withholding food and water.

Israel also continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza every day, despite a ceasefire signed in October.

Against this background, Israel seeks to portray the departure of Palestinians from Gaza as “voluntary”.

Under Ben Gvir’s plan, Israel would work to expel Palestinians to countries including Turkey, Ethiopia and Congo, as well as several Arab states.

The proposal would require “international partnership”, with participating countries accepting Palestinians expelled under the plan.

The Jewish Power leader will also set out the projected cost of his programme, which is likely to draw international condemnation.

The plan would cost more than $3bn in its first year and about $20bn in total over seven years.

Israel Katz says Palestinians will leave Gaza
Read More »

Ben Gvir is expected to make the proposal a condition for joining the next government. He currently serves in a coalition led by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Ben Gvir will also demand the appointment of a minister to oversee the forcible transfer of Palestinians, supported by a director general, a dedicated budget, extensive powers and an international negotiating team.

Ben Gvir’s announcement follows similar remarks from Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday.

“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without migration,” Katz said at a conference hosted by Israeli outlet Ynet in cooperation with the Israel Democracy Institute.

“What’s delaying it is that the accepting countries want US support. Every country that is willing wants American backing. Currently, President Trump didn’t cancel this; he froze it. All the Arab countries came to him due to their pressure on this matter,” Katz said.

At the end of June, Israel renamed its plan to forcibly transfer Palestinians from Gaza, abandoning the term “voluntary migration” in favour of “Freedom of Movement Plan”. The framework lacks provisions or guarantees for a right of return.
